text:
Round two. Most of you don't invest a lump sum. You invest every month.

So, three hundred euros a month, starting in January 2000. Straight into the crash.

By the end of 2002, you've put in ten thousand eight hundred euros. It's worth seven thousand two hundred.

By the end of 2008, after nine years of saving, thirty-two thousand four hundred in, twenty-three thousand four hundred left. That's the moment most people quit.

But those were the months when every three hundred euros bought the most shares. The crash years were your best buying years.

And look how fast that repaired the damage. The lump sum needed thirteen years to get back to ten thousand euros. The monthly plan was back above what you'd put in by the end of 2005, three years after the bottom. After 2008, it took two.

Today, you've put in ninety-six thousand euros. The plan is worth about four hundred and sixteen thousand.

Here's a twist. What if you had put the whole ninety-six thousand euros in at once, on the worst possible day, at the end of 1999?

It would be worth about four hundred and forty-two thousand today. Even at the very top, the lump sum beat the monthly plan, because the money spent longer in the market.

But almost nobody holds a lump sum through thirteen years under water. The monthly plan is the one people actually stick with, and that's worth more than the difference.

Now the version most people actually lived. Same plan, but you pause it from 2009 to 2013, because the news is terrible, and restart in 2014.

You saved eighteen thousand euros by pausing. And you ended with about one hundred and eight thousand euros less.

The five years you skipped were some of the cheapest prices of the whole century.

For a monthly saver, a crash isn't the danger. Stopping is.

There's a layer most European investors forget completely. The dollar.

More than seventy percent of your world ETF is priced in dollars. When the dollar falls against the euro, you lose money, even if American stocks don't move.

Buying the euro listed version of the ETF doesn't change that. What matters is the currency of the companies inside it.

In October 2000, one euro bought just eighty-three cents. By the end of 2004, it bought one dollar thirty-six.

That move alone wiped almost forty percent off every dollar asset, measured in euros.

Look at 2002. World stocks lost about twenty percent in dollars. In euros, they lost thirty-three.

Over the three crash years together, the world index lost forty-two percent in dollars, and almost forty-five in euros.

Then 2008 did the opposite. Investors ran to the dollar, and that cushioned the crash: minus forty-one percent in dollars, minus thirty-seven in euros.

In 2025 the dollar fell again. World stocks gained about twenty-one percent in dollars, but only seven percent for a euro investor.

Over the whole period, from 2000 to 2025, the index returned about three hundred and ninety-six percent in dollars, and three hundred and twenty-five in euros.

Over twenty-six years, a lot of it washed out. Over five or ten years, it can decide whether you made money at all.

Right now the euro is around one dollar thirteen, after both the Fed and the E C B raised rates in September. If the dollar falls while US stocks fall, you get hit twice.

Euro hedged share classes remove that risk. But they cost a bit more, and they also remove the airbag you had in 2008.
